pharm: Orally active local-anaesthetic-type antiarrhythmic that inhibits the fast inward sodium current, reducing the rate of rise of the cardiac action potential and shortening the action-potential duration and effective refractory period in Purkinje fibres
quick: Start 200 mg every 8 h; usual 200-300 mg every 8 h (max 1200 mg/day)
Take with food or an antacid to reduce gastrointestinal upset
Use only if the potential benefit justifies the risk; crosses placenta and enters milk
Excreted in breast milk at concentrations similar to plasma; use with caution
Patients with renal failure generally require the usual doses
Severe liver disease may require lower doses; monitor closely (hepatic metabolism)
Avoid excess; additive CNS effects and possible altered metabolism
ECG/rhythm, blood pressure, liver function, plasma levels if needed
summary: Mexiletine is an orally active class IB antiarrhythmic, structurally similar to lidocaine, indicated for the treatment of documented ventricular arrhythmias - such as sustained ventricular tachycardia - that are, in the physician's judgement, life-threatening. Because of its proarrhythmic effects it should not be used for lesser or asymptomatic arrhythmias, and treatment should be started in hospital. Therapy is begun at 200 mg every 8 hours (with food or antacid), with dose adjustments of 50-100 mg no more often than every 2-3 days; most patients are controlled on 200-300 mg every 8 hours, and the dose should not exceed 1200 mg/day. The CAST trial showed excess mortality with class I antiarrhythmics in patients with non-life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias after myocardial infarction, and no antiarrhythmic has been shown to improve survival in such patients, so use is reserved for life-threatening arrhythmias. Post-marketing reports of abnormal liver function tests, sometimes early in therapy and mostly in heart failure or ischaemia, warrant liver monitoring.
indications: Treatment of documented, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias such as sustained ventricular tachycardia
Use for lesser or asymptomatic ventricular arrhythmias is generally not recommended because of proarrhythmic effects

dosage.d: 200 mg every 8 hours when rapid control is not essential
dosage.t: Every 8 hours with food or antacid; start in hospital
dosage.n: Allow at least 2-3 days between dose changes; adjust in 50-100 mg increments

dosage.d: Usually 200 to 300 mg every 8 hours; if inadequate and tolerated, may try 400 mg every 8 hours
dosage.t: Every 8 hours with food or antacid
dosage.n: Do not exceed 1200 mg/day (CNS side effects increase with total daily dose)

dosage.c: Adult - hepatic impairment / severe right heart failure
dosage.d: May require lower doses than usual; titrate carefully
dosage.n: Monitor closely; right-sided CHF reduces hepatic metabolism

admin: Initiate therapy in hospital with continuous ECG monitoring because of proarrhythmic risk
Administer with food or an antacid to reduce gastrointestinal upset and to standardise absorption
Allow a minimum of 2-3 days between dose adjustments and titrate to clinical and ECG (including Holter) response
Use the lowest effective dose; reduce the dose for severe hepatic disease or marked right-sided heart failure
Avoid abrupt changes in urinary pH (severe urinary alkalinisation can substantially reduce excretion)
moa: Mexiletine is a class IB (lidocaine-like) antiarrhythmic and local anaesthetic. It inhibits the fast inward sodium current, reducing the maximum rate of rise of phase 0 of the cardiac action potential, particularly in depolarised and ischaemic tissue. In Purkinje fibres it shortens the action-potential duration to a greater extent than the effective refractory period, increasing the ERP/APD ratio. In patients with normal conduction it has minimal effect on impulse generation and propagation and does not prolong the QRS or QT interval, so it may be useful for ventricular arrhythmias associated with a prolonged QT. It suppresses ventricular ectopy and re-entrant ventricular tachyarrhythmias.

absolute: Pre-existing second- or third-degree AV block in the absence of a functioning pacemaker
relative: Pre-existing sinus node dysfunction or first-degree AV block / intraventricular conduction abnormalities
Hypotension and severe congestive heart failure
Seizure disorder (CNS toxicity can lower threshold)
monitor: Liver function tests, especially in the first weeks
Plasma mexiletine levels when toxicity or non-response is suspected

preg: There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Mexiletine crosses the placenta and should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Mexiletine is excreted in human milk at concentrations similar to those in plasma. Because of the potential for adverse effects in the nursing infant, use with caution and weigh the benefit of breastfeeding against the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: Patients with renal failure generally require the usual doses of mexiletine. Severe alkalinisation of the urine can markedly reduce renal excretion, while marked acidification increases it.
hepatic: Mexiletine is metabolised in the liver, and hepatic impairment prolongs its elimination. Patients with severe liver disease (and those with marked right-sided congestive heart failure, which reduces hepatic metabolism) may require lower doses and should be monitored closely. Abnormal liver function tests, including hepatic injury, have been reported, sometimes within the first weeks of therapy.

major: Other antiarrhythmics and QRS/QT-affecting drugs - additive proarrhythmic and cardiac depressant effects
moderate: CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g. fluvoxamine) and CYP2D6 inhibitors - raise mexiletine levels
Hepatic enzyme inducers (phenytoin, rifampicin, phenobarbital) - lower mexiletine plasma levels
Theophylline - mexiletine increases theophylline levels (risk of theophylline toxicity)
minor: Narcotics, atropine and antacids - delay mexiletine absorption (do not reduce total absorbed amount)
interactions.food: Take with food or antacid to reduce gastric upset; large changes in urinary pH alter excretion
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol - additive CNS effects
interactions.diagnostics: Generally does not prolong QRS or QT on the ECG; monitor liver function tests

common: Nervousness, changes in sleep, blurred vision, headache
serious: Proarrhythmia - worsening of ventricular arrhythmia (greater concern with life-threatening arrhythmias)
Hepatic injury / abnormal liver function tests
Aggravation of hypotension and congestive heart failure
rare: Severe skin reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome / erythema multiforme
emergency: Sustained or worsening ventricular tachyarrhythmia / cardiovascular collapse

monitoring: Continuous ECG during initiation and periodic ECG/Holter thereafter
Blood pressure and signs of worsening heart failure
Liver function tests, particularly during the first weeks of therapy
Complete blood count if blood dyscrasia is suspected
Plasma mexiletine concentration when toxicity or inadequate response is suspected
counsel: This medicine controls a serious, life-threatening heart rhythm problem and must be taken exactly as prescribed
Take it with food or an antacid to reduce stomach upset
Report tremor, dizziness, unsteadiness, severe stomach upset, yellowing of skin/eyes, fever or rash
Do not stop or change the dose suddenly without medical advice
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, including for epilepsy, asthma (theophylline) and caffeine intake
pk: Oral absorption is rapid and nearly complete; antiarrhythmic effect develops over hours to a few days of titration
Plasma peak about 2-3 hours after an oral dose
Elimination half-life about 10-12 hours (prolonged in hepatic impairment or heart failure)
Dosing every 8 hours maintains therapeutic plasma levels
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from excessive heat and moisture
pearls: Class IB (lidocaine-like) - shortens action-potential duration and does not prolong QRS/QT; can suit long-QT-associated VT
Reserve for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and start in hospital (CAST trial: excess mortality with class I agents post-MI)
Give with food/antacid; CNS side effects (tremor, dizziness) are dose-related and limit total daily dose to 1200 mg
Hepatically cleared - lower doses in severe liver disease or marked right heart failure; monitor LFTs early
Raises theophylline levels and reduces caffeine clearance; enzyme inducers lower mexiletine levels
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; in that case skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses at once. Keep taking the medicine on schedule and do not stop without medical advice.
overdose: Overdose may cause drowsiness, confusion, nausea, hypotension, sinus bradycardia, paraesthesia, seizures, bundle-branch block, AV block, asystole, ventricular tachyarrhythmia (including fibrillation), cardiovascular collapse and coma. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive with close monitoring of vital signs; pressor agents, atropine or anticonvulsants and transvenous cardiac pacing may be used depending on the clinical picture. Acidification of the urine can increase elimination.
